"竞争、模仿、相互影响：自19世纪诞生以来，摄影与绘画之间便维持着一种含混不清的关系。例如，印象派画家拒绝与相机的机械精确性竞争，而是将一切押注在感官、光线以及稍纵即逝的时刻上。他们试图发明自己的语言，并摆脱对现实的单纯再现。历史具有讽刺意味的是，几十年后，画意摄影师（Pictorialist）却尝试走向反面，创作出具有近乎绘画般氛围的柔焦影像，迎合了画笔的质感与笔触。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如沃尔特·本雅明（Walter Benjamin）在《机械复制时代的艺术作品》（1936年）中所观察到的那样，摄影的出现颠覆了人们对艺术的感知。如今可以无限复制的影像动摇了独一无二作品的“神韵”（aura），迫使绘画在面对这双全新的机械之眼时，重新思考其媒介并实现自我重塑。当相机以画笔无法企及的精确度捕捉到瞬间时，绘画必须寻找其他路径、其他强度以及其他留住时间的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今天，历史似乎走了一个轮回，轮到摄影开始向绘画寻求自我重塑了。这种绘画参考不再是模仿，而成了一种思考影像的方式。在一个影像接踵而至、让人应接不暇的世界里，在无限滚动浏览和算法塑造我们注意力的时代，一些摄影师选择放慢脚步，将每一张影像锚定在时间和空间之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/7.zoe--coral-snake-jpg-1024x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "珊瑚蛇 © Zoë Zimmerman", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2.zoe--pandemic17--1024x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "大流行 #17 © Zoë Zimmerman", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/1.zoe--quarantine57-1-819x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "隔离 #57 © Zoë Zimmerman", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/4.zoe--pandemic-89--866x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "大流行 #89 © Zoë Zimmerman", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这场绘画与摄影的对话中，一些地标性的作品脱颖而出。在她的系列作品“Xteriors”中，荷兰摄影师黛西丽·多尔龙（Desiree Dolron）探索了介于肖像画与风景画之间的领域。她的影像通常沐浴在漫射光中，背景极具戏剧张力，让人联想到巴洛克绘画。人物在沉稳或黑暗的背景衬托下显得格外突出，仿佛悬浮在时间之中，而雕塑般的光线则让人想起卡拉瓦乔（Caravaggio）或佛兰德斯大师（Flemish masters）。另一方面，莱蒂蒂亚·莫尔纳（Laetitia Molenaar）则将爱德华·霍珀（Edward Hopper）的画作作为其艺术项目的起点。在她名为《Here Comes The Sun》的系列中，风景和人物变成了运动中的画作，每一个画幅都在讲述一个故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "相反，当代画家如彼得·多伊格（Peter Doig）和格哈德·里希特（Gerhard Richter）则让摄影的痕迹在他们的画布上隐现。通过转换、叠加和混合，这两种媒介在无休止的创作往复中相互滋养。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "失而复得的时间", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于美国摄影师佐伊·齐默尔曼（Zoë Zimmerman）而言，她与绘画的关系甚至更为直接。她近期的作品明确借鉴了16世纪和17世纪的静物画。她的构图通常在自然光下以暗色背景拍摄，直接唤起了卡拉瓦乔的遗产。这种构图感归功于她多年来对绘画的凝视：“什么能满足我的眼光？画家的视角：放弃那些在摄影中占主导地位的巧妙角度和复杂布光。自然光一直是我最简单的解法。一个暗背景，加上来自一个清晰方向的侧射光，洒在主体上（无论那是什么）……然后你就会发现：这就是卡拉瓦乔！”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但这种绘画参考不仅停留在美学层面。它还关乎影像的构思方式。佐伊·齐默尔曼谈到了一种“前摄影视觉”（pre-photographic vision）：在这种构图中，影像的每一个平面都承载着相同的视觉分量。不同于现代摄影习惯于模糊背景和浅景深，她追求整体的清晰度，这让人想起维米尔（Vermeer）画作的结构。“这就是艺术家在镜头艺术教导我们接受模糊背景和柔焦物体作为它们在画幅中重要性较低的标志之前，构建其构图的方式。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "直到2020年，她的作品一直严格采用黑白胶片，使用大画幅相机拍摄。当她涉足彩色摄影时，她表现得十分谨慎。“我发现自己一次只能处理一两种主色调。我被以前作品中根本不存在的选择弄得应接不暇。随着时间的推移，我的调色板拓宽了，但我仍然倾向于有限且偏暗的色调。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
Rivalry, imitation, mutual influence: since its beginnings in the 19th century, photography has maintained an ambiguous relationship with painting. The Impressionists, for instance, refused to compete with the camera’s mechanical precision and staked everything on sensation, light and the fleeting moment. They sought to invent their own language and move away from the mere reproduction of reality. In an irony of history, a few decades later the Pictorialist photographers attempted the opposite, producing soft-focus images with almost painterly atmospheres that flirted with the texture and gesture of the brush.

As Walter Benjamin observed in The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1936), the advent of photography upended the perception of art. Images, now reproducible ad infinitum, shook the aura of the unique work, forcing painting to rethink its means and reinvent itself in the face of this new mechanical eye. Where the camera captured the moment with a precision the brush could not match, painting had to find other paths, other intensities, other ways of holding on to time.

Today, history seems to have come full circle, and it is photography that looks to painting to reinvent itself. The pictorial reference is no longer imitation; it has become a way of thinking about the image. In a world where images follow one another faster than they can be looked at, where infinite scrolling and algorithms shape our attention, some photographers are choosing to slow down, anchoring each image in time and space.

Landmarks emerge in this dialogue between painting and photography. In her series “Xteriors,” Dutch photographer Desiree Dolron explores territory on the border between portraiture and landscape. Her images, often bathed in diffuse light against dramatic backgrounds, evoke Baroque paintings. Bodies stand out against neutral or dark grounds, as if suspended in time, and the sculpted light recalls Caravaggio or the Flemish masters. Laetitia Molenaar, for her part, took Edward Hopper’s paintings as the starting point for her artistic project. In her series Here Comes The Sun , landscapes and figures become paintings in motion, where every frame tells a story.

Conversely, contemporary painters such as Peter Doig and Gerhard Richter let photographic traces float through their canvases. Through shifts, overlays and hybridizations, the two mediums feed off each other in an endless creative back-and-forth.

Time regained

For the American photographer Zoë Zimmerman, the relationship with painting is even more direct. Her recent work draws explicitly on the still lifes of the 16th and 17th centuries. Her compositions, often made in natural light against a dark background, immediately evoke the legacy of Caravaggio. It is a sense of composition she owes to years spent contemplating paintings: “What satisfies my eye? The painter’s point of view: giving up the clever angles and complicated lighting that dominate so much of photography. Natural light has always been my simplest solution. A dark background and raking light coming from one clear direction, falling across the subject (whatever it may be)… and there you have it: Caravaggio!”

But the pictorial reference is not merely aesthetic. It also concerns the way the image is conceived. Zoë Zimmerman speaks of a “pre-photographic vision”: a composition in which every plane of the image carries equal visual weight. Unlike modern photography, accustomed to blurred backgrounds and shallow depth of field, she aims for overall sharpness, recalling the structure of Vermeer’s paintings. “This is how artists built their compositions before lens-based art taught us to accept blurred backgrounds and soft objects as signs of their lesser importance within the frame.”

Until 2020, her work was strictly black and white, shot on film with a large-format view camera. When she ventured into color, she did so cautiously. “I found that I could only handle one or two dominant colors at a time. I was overwhelmed by choices that simply did not exist in my earlier work. My palette has broadened over time, but I still lean toward something limited and dark.”

In her series “Covid Vanitas,” these compositions even become a discreet commentary on the pandemic. Created during an unprecedented global period of isolation and apprehension, her images carry social commentary in the manner of a subplot. The photographs contain clues to the era: plastic market bags left in with the fruit, a banana taped to the wall in the background, a profusion of dead birds that symbolize lost hope but are also, quite literally, a consequence of climate change… Each detail lifts the pictures out of a backward-looking aesthetic sentimentality and places them within the stakes of the present. The markers of contemporary daily life play supporting roles in a body of work devoted to the artist’s inner life, but they are essential to keeping the work in the “now” while moving it forward.

In her still lifes, objects also become contemporary symbols. “Still life as a genre can be predictable and hollow, or simply aim for pretty,” she says. “The best of my work is a reflection of my inner life, expressing emotions or concepts in the moment. Objects are chosen to best express a non-physical subject. Sometimes it is their color, their outline or their shape. Sometimes it is less ambiguous: lemons symbolizing the bitterness of life, or a plastic bag rendered like silk, reminding us that what we throw away so easily will be our undoing. Other things, however, serve only as compositional elements: there is no metaphor. The image simply needs a piece of tape…”

In praise of slowness

This return to a form of slowness is no coincidence in a world saturated with images. For Zoë Zimmerman, the photographic image is first and foremost a material object. “My photographs are made to be seen as prints on paper,” she explains. “We are all inundated with images shared on screens, including paintings, which are best seen in their subtle three-dimensionality. It saddens me that the photographic print is a dying art.”

On screen, they lose their duende , a term borrowed from Hispanic culture that refers to an almost mysterious intensity, a deep emotional vibration. Zimmerman associates this quality with the materiality and depth of ink on paper. This paradox perhaps sums up what is at stake for photography today: making images at a time when they have become infinitely reproducible.

Although her practice runs counter to instantaneity, Zoë Zimmerman does not reject digital technology, acknowledging that “sharing an image immediately and widely is extraordinary, allowing those of us who create in remote regions to distribute our work globally.”

Faced with the endless scroll, some photographers are attempting to reintroduce a slower way of looking, close to the experience one has in front of a painting. Rather than disappearing amid the proliferation of images, photography today seems to be rediscovering certain qualities that painting long cultivated: composition, materiality, the duration of the gaze.

In this renewed dialogue between the two mediums, the pictorial reference is not nostalgic. It becomes a critical tool for rethinking what it means to make an image in the age of instantaneity and artificial intelligence. Slowing down, composing, looking: these gestures may well, paradoxically, be among the most contemporary forms of photography. Zoë Zimmerman’s words capture this impulse: “I hope my images encourage people to slow down in this relentless scrolling. To really see something. And perhaps to feel something.”
